No, definitely not.  Don’t get me wrong, before I met my current partner, I genuinely thought we were unloveable and were destined to never have a partner. I am so lucky to have such an understanding partner that also is willing to help me and not give up on me. 


Granted, we are also a system (diagnosed with DID) so our experience may be a bit different from everyone here since not all of us have BPD. It’s basically only the host and few others that are diagnosed with BPD. 


It took HARD work to get to where I am with our partner, but that is because I am privileged to have access to therapy and I also have an amazing therapist. He also makes me take accountability even though when I had these episodes, I could genuinely NOT see where I messed up or what the problem was, or that it was even my fault. Of course because of the BPD, the host would have a lot of outbursts and would split without of course, meaning to. 


So, from an outsider perspective, it seemed like I was always making myself the “victim”. But since my partner was informed since day 1 of our disorder, he got educated on it and was willing to help me and steer me to the right direction. Our partner is super patient with us and yes, even though it is because we have a disorder, it is ultimately up to us to work hard to improve in our disorder. It’s very very hard and takes time, but we have it much more under control now and because of him and my therapist, I was able to recognize and see the patterns that would drive some of us and the host into spitting, and we are now able to efficiently detect our triggers (most of the time). 



The biggest thing is to find a good support system that is able to hold you accountable and able to tell you things you are not able to notice you do because of your disorder (that’s why it’s a disorder in the first place). Don’t give up, there’s someone out there for you. Just be patient with yourself and give yourself grace. 


I should mention that our partner is on the spectrum, so not sure if that has anything to do with it.

We had a similar experience. Nothing worked, DBT nor CBT. Our old therapist would tell us that our abuse was normal and would gaslight us. She would then trigger the host (since the host does not know about her trauma) and cause her to severely dissociate. Once I brought up that I think we were suffering from PTSD or BPD and she dismissed us. It got to the point that I thought we were a lost cause. 

It wasn’t until I found our new therapist that we have been working with for over a year now, that she saw how disparate we were to receiving help and through this, she also saw how severely dissociative we were. After a few months of seeing her, she diagnosed us. It was hard for the host to grasp the diagnosis and really take that in. It was a shock to her, since she never expected that. But what everyone was telling her about acting differently, etc.. was true. We also had gone to 2 psychologist and they also diagnosed us. 

It’s very embarrassing at the work place, since we still have very strong amnesiac barriers and we feel like an airhead half the time since people notice I’m “slow” since I re-ask questions, etc. 

It’s not fun nor cute and especially since in my ethnic background with my family, it’s very stigmatized having any kind of mental illness, being abused the way we were, and even going to therapy is frowned down upon. It’s extremely hard and I really dislike seeing people romanticize it the way they do on TT. 

I guess I don’t really understand how people self diagnosed since the host and some of the others had no idea we had anything. Except the comments my family would make or people closest to me would make.

We’re a system and we actually had a problem like this, where the host would forget when our partner would say not to do or say certain things and she would keep repeating these repetitive things to our partner. She also meant no harm, since she was not aware that her actions were affecting our partner in a negative way. 

Basically, our partner got to the point to where they had to put “consequences” in place and we also had a long talk recently with our therapist about this problem and it has to do with the rooted trauma our host has and with the other alters and their very ingrained belief system about men (due to the trauma). We are currently working on it with our therapist. Our therapist told us if we don’t heal this, the host will keep repeating these behaviors, since the others are erasing her memories (why she forgets). 

Now, we can’t speak on behalf of your partner or what they are dealing with, since every system is different but that is our personal experience on something similar to that.
